lessons.title: Choosing the Right Spot: Size, Shade, and Water Access
lessons.body: Choosing the right spot for your compost heap is the first step to success. In Africa, where sun can be intense, you need a place that gets some shade during the hottest part of the day. Partial shade from a tree or building is ideal. Full sun will dry out your heap too fast, and full shade might keep it too cool and slow decomposition. Aim for a spot that gets morning sun and afternoon shade. The size of your heap matters: a heap that is too small (less than 1 cubic meter) won't heat up enough, while one that is too large (over 2 cubic meters) is hard to turn. A good size for a household is about 1 meter wide by 1 meter high by 1 meter deep. That's roughly 1 cubic meter. You also need easy access to water. Compost needs moisture, so choose a spot within 10-15 meters of a water source, like a tap, well, or rainwater tank. If you have to carry water far, you'll be less likely to keep the heap properly moist. Also, make sure the spot is level and well-drained. If water pools around the heap, it can become soggy and smelly. Avoid low spots where rain collects. Finally, consider convenience: you want to be able to add materials regularly without a long walk. A spot near your kitchen garden or where you process crops is ideal. Clear the area of weeds and grass, and loosen the soil underneath to allow worms and microbes to enter. If you have problems with termites, place a layer of gravel or broken bricks at the base. With the right spot, you're ready to build.

lessons.title: Layering Browns and Greens: The Ideal Ratio
lessons.body: The secret to a hot, fast-working compost heap is the right mix of 'browns' and 'greens'. Browns are dry, carbon-rich materials like dry leaves, straw, hay, maize stalks, sawdust, shredded paper, and cardboard. Greens are wet, nitrogen-rich materials like fresh grass clippings, vegetable scraps, fruit peels, coffee grounds, tea leaves, and animal manure (from cows, goats, chickens, but not dogs or cats). The ideal ratio is about 2 to 3 parts browns to 1 part greens by volume. That means for every bucket of greens, add 2-3 buckets of browns. If you have too many greens, the heap becomes slimy, smells like ammonia, and attracts flies. Too many browns, and it decomposes very slowly. To build the heap, start with a 15-20 cm layer of coarse browns like maize stalks or small twigs at the bottom for drainage and airflow. Then add a layer of greens, about 10-15 cm thick. Sprinkle a little soil or old compost on topâthis adds microorganisms. Then add a layer of browns, 15-20 cm thick. Repeat these layers: greens, soil, browns, until the heap is about 1 meter high. Each time you add a layer, water it lightly to keep it moist like a wrung-out sponge. If you have manure, mix it with the greens. Chop large pieces into smaller bitsâthis speeds up decomposition. Turn the heap after a week to mix the layers. If you notice a bad smell, add more browns. If it's too dry, add water and more greens. With the right ratio, your heap will heat up within 2-3 days, reaching temperatures of 55-65Â°C, which kills weed seeds and pathogens.

lessons.title: Adding Water: How to Test Moisture by Hand
lessons.body: Water is the lifeblood of your compost heap. Without enough moisture, the microbes that break down organic matter slow down and stop. With too much, the heap becomes waterlogged, anaerobic (without oxygen), and smells like rotten eggs. The goal is to keep the heap as moist as a wrung-out sponge. To test moisture by hand, stick your hand into the middle of the heap and pull out a handful of material. Squeeze it firmly in your fist. If it drips water, it's too wetâadd more browns and turn it. If it feels dry and crumbles apart, it's too dryâadd water and turn it. If it feels like a damp sponge and only a few drops come out, it's perfect. You should check moisture every 2-3 days, especially in hot, dry weather. In Africa, where temperatures can soar, you may need to water every day. Use a watering can or hose with a gentle spray to avoid compacting the heap. Add water slowly, letting it soak in. If you live in a rainy area, you may need to cover the heap with a tarp or banana leaves to prevent it from getting too wet. During the rainy season, check moisture less often. If the heap is too wet, turn it to add air and mix in dry browns. A simple tool: a stick or machete inserted into the heap can help you feel the moisture at different depths. Remember, the center of the heap should be as moist as the edges. If the edges are dry, push them toward the center when you turn. Consistent moisture is key to fast composting.

lessons.title: Building a Heap with a Pallet or Wire Bin
lessons.body: You can build a compost heap with simple materials found around your home or farm. Two popular methods are using wooden pallets or a wire bin. For a pallet bin, collect four wooden pallets of the same size. Stand three pallets on edge to form a U-shape, and tie them together at the corners with wire or rope. Drive wooden stakes or metal posts into the ground at the corners for support. The fourth pallet can be used as a removable front, so you can easily turn and harvest the compost. If you don't have pallets, use a wire bin: buy a roll of wire mesh (chicken wire or welded wire) at least 1 meter high. Form it into a circle about 1 meter in diameter, and secure the ends with wire. You can also use wooden stakes to hold it in place. The advantage of a wire bin is good airflow, but it can dry out faster, so monitor moisture. For both methods, place the bin on level ground, preferably on soil, not concrete, so worms and microbes can enter. If you have termites, place a layer of gravel at the base. Start your heap by adding a 15 cm layer of coarse browns at the bottom. Then alternate greens and browns as described in Lesson 2. With a pallet bin, you can remove the front pallet to turn the heap easily. With a wire bin, you can simply lift the wire and move it to the side, then fork the compost back into the bin. Turn the heap every 1-2 weeks. In hot, dry areas, you may need to water more often. These bins are cheap, easy to build, and can be made from recycled materials. They keep your heap neat and make turning and harvesting much easier.

lessons.title: Turning Schedule: When and How Often
lessons.body: Turning your compost heap is like stirring a pot of stewâit mixes everything, adds oxygen, and speeds up decomposition. The general rule is to turn the heap every 1-2 weeks for the first month, then every 2-3 weeks until it's finished. But the schedule depends on your goals. If you want compost fast (in 1-2 months), turn every 3-4 days. If you're not in a hurry, turn every 2-4 weeks. How do you know when to turn? Stick a metal rod or long stick into the center of the heap. Leave it for 10 minutes, then pull it out. If it's hot to the touch, the heap is active and doesn't need turning yet. If it's warm or cool, it's time to turn. Also, if the heap starts to smell bad or looks matted, turn it. To turn, use a pitchfork or shovel. Start by pulling materials from the outside to the center, and from the top to the bottom. Mix thoroughly. If the heap is too dry, add water as you turn. If too wet, add dry browns. If you have a pallet bin with a removable front, simply remove the front, fork the material into a new pile beside it, then put it back. With a wire bin, lift the wire off, set it aside, and fork the compost back into the wire. After turning, reshape the heap into a dome. In hot African climates, turning may dry out the heap, so water after turning. If you turn too often, you might disrupt the heating process. If you turn too little, it becomes anaerobic. Aim for a balance. A well-turned heap will heat up again within a day after turning. Keep a simple calendar or mark on a stick to remind you when to turn.

lessons.title: Harvesting Finished Compost: Signs and Timing
lessons.body: After weeks of layering, watering, and turning, your compost is ready to harvest when it looks and smells like rich, dark soil. The signs are clear: the heap no longer heats up, even after turning. The original materials are mostly unrecognizableâyou can't tell a banana peel from a leaf. It has a sweet, earthy smell, like forest floor after rain. It's crumbly and cool to the touch. The volume is about half to one-third of what you started with. Depending on your climate and how often you turned, this can take 1-3 months in hot weather, or 4-6 months in cooler conditions. To harvest, stop adding new materials to the heap about 2-3 weeks before you expect it to finish. This lets the last additions decompose. If you have a pallet or wire bin, remove the bin and let the pile sit for a few days. Then, use a fork or shovel to move the compost to a screen or sieve. A simple screen can be made with wire mesh over a wooden frame. Sift the compost to remove any large, unfinished piecesâthese can go back into the next heap. The finished compost is ready to use. Store it in sacks or a covered pile in a dry place. Use it in your garden by mixing it into the soil at planting, or as a top dressing. You can also make compost tea by soaking a sack of compost in water for a day. Never use compost that still has recognizable food scraps or smells sourâit's not ready. With practice, you'll learn to judge the perfect timing.

quiz.q: What is the ideal size for a household compost heap?
quiz.explanation: A heap of about 1 cubic meter (1m x 1m x 1m) is large enough to heat up but manageable to turn.

quiz.q: Why should you choose a spot with partial shade for your compost heap?
options: A) To keep it cool and slow decomposition
B) To prevent it from drying out too fast
quiz.explanation: Partial shade prevents the heap from drying out too quickly in hot climates while still allowing some warmth.

quiz.q: How far should your compost heap be from a water source?
quiz.explanation: Easy access to water within 10-15 meters makes it convenient to keep the heap properly moist.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ratio of browns to greens in a compost heap?
options: B) 2-3 parts browns to 1 part greens
C) 1 part browns to 2-3 parts greens
D) 5 parts browns to 1 part greens
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 2-3 parts browns to 1 part greens by volume provides the right carbon-to-nitrogen balance.

quiz.q: Which of the following is considered a 'green' material for composting?
quiz.explanation: Fresh grass clippings are nitrogen-rich and count as greens.

quiz.q: What should you do if your compost heap smells like ammonia?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia smell indicates too many greens; adding browns balances the ratio.

quiz.q: How thick should the first layer of coarse browns be at the bottom of the heap?
quiz.explanation: A 15-20 cm layer of coarse browns provides drainage and airflow.

quiz.q: What temperature range indicates an active, hot compost heap?
quiz.explanation: A temperature of 55-65Â°C kills weed seeds and pathogens and shows rapid decomposition.

quiz.q: How can you test if your compost heap has the right moisture?
options: A) Squeeze a handful and see if it drips
B) Pour a bucket of water on it
C) Check if it's dry on top
quiz.explanation: The squeeze test: if it feels like a wrung-out sponge with few drops, moisture is ideal.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a squeezed handful of compost drips water?
quiz.explanation: Dripping water indicates excess moisture; add browns and turn.

quiz.q: How often should you check the moisture of your compost heap in hot, dry weather?
quiz.explanation: In hot, dry conditions, moisture evaporates quickly, so check every 2-3 days.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to check moisture at different depths in the heap?
quiz.explanation: Inserting a stick or machete helps you feel moisture at various depths.

quiz.q: What material can be used to build a compost bin?
quiz.explanation: Both pallets and wire mesh are commonly used to build compost bins.

quiz.q: Why is it recommended to place a compost bin on soil rather than concrete?
options: A) To prevent it from blowing away
B) To allow worms and microbes to enter
D) To make it easier to turn
quiz.explanation: Soil contact allows beneficial organisms like worms and microbes to enter the heap.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of a wire bin over a pallet bin?
quiz.explanation: Wire bins provide good airflow, which helps aerobic decomposition.

quiz.q: How can you easily turn compost in a pallet bin?
quiz.explanation: A removable front pallet allows easy access to fork and turn the compost.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have termites in your area when building a compost heap?
options: B) Place a layer of gravel at the base
C) Build it far from the house
quiz.explanation: A gravel layer can deter termites from entering the heap from the ground.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost heap if you want fast compost?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 3-4 days speeds up decomposition for faster compost.

quiz.q: What is a sign that it's time to turn the compost heap?
options: B) The heap is warm or cool
quiz.explanation: When the heap cools down, it needs turning to reintroduce oxygen and restart heating.

quiz.q: How can you tell if the compost heap is too dry when turning?
options: A) It crumbles and feels dry
D) It's hot in the center
quiz.explanation: Dry compost crumbles; add water while turning to restore moisture.

quiz.q: What should you do after turning the heap in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: Turning exposes moist material to air, so water after turning to maintain moisture.

quiz.q: What is a good way to remember when to turn your compost?
options: A) Use a calendar or mark on a stick
B) Turn it every time you pass by
C) Turn it only when it smells
D) Turn it once a year
quiz.explanation: Keeping a simple calendar or mark helps you stick to a turning schedule.

quiz.q: What are the signs that compost is ready to harvest?
options: A) It still heats up after turning
B) It has a sweet, earthy smell
C) You can recognize food scraps
quiz.explanation: Finished compost has a sweet, earthy smell and no longer heats up.

quiz.q: How long does it typically take to make compost in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: In hot climates with regular turning, compost can be ready in 1-3 months.

quiz.q: What should you do before harvesting compost?
options: B) Stop adding new materials for 2-3 weeks
quiz.explanation: Stopping additions allows the last materials to decompose fully before harvest.

quiz.q: How can you remove large, unfinished pieces from finished compost?
options: A) Use a sieve or screen
B) Pick them out by hand
quiz.explanation: Sifting through a screen separates finished compost from larger pieces that can be recomposted.

quiz.q: How should you store finished compost?
options: A) In sacks in a dry place
D) In a sealed plastic bag
quiz.explanation: Store in sacks or a covered pile in a dry place to preserve quality.

quiz.q: What is compost tea?
options: B) Soaking compost in water to make liquid fertilizer
quiz.explanation: Compost tea is made by soaking a sack of compost in water, creating a nutrient-rich liquid for plants.

quiz.q: Why should you not use compost that still has recognizable food scraps?
options: A) It's not ready and may harm plants
quiz.explanation: Unfinished compost can attract pests, smell, and may not be safe for plants.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture consistency of compost?
quiz.explanation: The wrung-out sponge analogy means moist but not dripping, ideal for microbial activity.
